title: UNICEF says thousands of children require mental health support after Nepal floods - UN News
description: UNICEF says thousands of children require mental health support after Nepal floods  UN News
publisher.title: UN News
full_article:
Triggered by glacier collapse, the 26 August floods affected more than 84,000 Nepalis – including about 32,000 children – and damaged critical roads, schools, power grids and water systems across the Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading regions of northern Nepal.

Local authorities report more than 1,300 killed and more than 5,000 still missing on the Nepal side of the border, and at least 43 people killed and 519 still missing on the Tibetan side, according to official Chinese Government figures.

Tweet URL

Many children affected by the floods witnessed the loss of loved ones and the destruction of their schools while some remain displaced from their communities.

Some 541 children remain separated from their families and require protection, UNICEF reported.

“Beyond the visible destruction, these floods have left deep emotional scars on children and families,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative in Nepal. “Alongside humanitarian supplies and restoration of critical infrastructure, children need mental health and psychosocial support to help them process what happened, regain a sense of security and begin to recover.”

Why mental health support?

The flooding began at 8:37am local time – at the beginning of the school day for many children.

According to Ms. Akunga, those who witnessed distressing events are now struggling with fear, anxiety and grief, with some unable to speak about what they experienced.

Shitanshu Dhakal, a medical doctor at a hospital in Nuwakot and a mental health advocate, described the “invisible burden” of trauma on flood-affected children and the fear many still feel long after the floods.

“Children must be at the centre of the mental health response, with immediate psychological first aid and sustained support to prevent long-term consequences,” Dr. Dhakal said.

UNICEF also highlighted the importance of acting quickly. Evidence shows that early mental health intervention is critical because it can stop acute stress from becoming a lifelong chronic disorder.

Support on the ground

On the ground in Nepal, UNICEF is working with the Nepal Government and other partners to support children through family tracing, reunification and mental health services.

Eighteen children have already been reunified with their families, and 13 UNICEF-supported Child-Friendly Spaces have been established.

UNICEF is helping to arrange alternative family-based care for youngsters who have lost both parents, and monitoring teams are working to identify those at-risk and prevent exploitation.

Meanwhile, Education Cannot Wait (ECW) – the UN’s global fund for education in emergencies – announced on Tuesday a $1 million allocation to support 17,000 children across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Of those, 5,000 will receive education and protection support, while 12,000 will benefit from risk reduction interventions.

Still, with nine schools severely damaged or destroyed, ECW said Nepal’s education system will require more funding from governments, foundations and the private sector to fully rebuild from the floods.

“With climate-related emergencies disrupting children’s education with increasing frequency, we must ensure that a temporary crisis does not turn into permanent learning loss,” ECW Director of Education Maysa Jalbout said.

title: MrBeast and Beast Philanthropy join CARE to help families recover from Nepal's floods - care.org
description: MrBeast and Beast Philanthropy join CARE to help families recover from Nepal's floods  care.org
publisher.title: care.org
full_article:
When the flood came through Ward 8 in Belkotgadhi in Nuwakot on August 26 , Sita watched years of hard work disappear.

In a matter of hours, her farmland was inundated. The maize and rice crops her family depended on were swept away.

For now, her family is staying with acquaintances on higher ground with no clear sense of when life will begin to feel normal again.

The CARE PACKAGE for Emergencies , CARE’s portable package, addresses the things Sita’s family needs now. Designed to support the needs of a family of four for a month, it is five kits in one :

A shelter kit with fireproof tarps and ropes for setting up a temporary shelter A wash kit with hygiene supplies and containers for portable bathing A kitchen kit with pots and a portable stove A dignity kit with sanitary pads and undergarments An energy kit with a solar charger and emergency light

Each of the up to 40 items is chosen for what families need in the weeks after a disaster, not just the first hours.

“It’s holistic, comprehensive,” Sita says of the CARE PACKAGE for Emergencies.

Namrata, a local government public employee who lives in Ward 7 in Belkotgadhi, has spent years helping residents access services and support. When the floods damaged her house, she came to a holding center, not knowing when it would be safe for her to return home again.

She points to some of the everyday items included in the CARE PACKAGE for Emergencies: toothpaste, matchsticks, and a lighter.

“Many don’t even think to include [these items],” she says.

For the 2,532 people who are sheltering across 33 holding centers like the one where Namrata is staying, having a CARE PACKAGE for Emergencies kit doesn’t just address survival needs. It includes items that provide dignity and a sense of normalcy.

title: Nepal Floods Left 268 Classrooms in Ruins. A New Scholarship Bank Aims to Rebuild What's Lost - Smiley Movement
description: Nepal Floods Left 268 Classrooms in Ruins. A New Scholarship Bank Aims to Rebuild What's Lost  Smiley Movement
publisher.title: Smiley Movement
full_article:
For two weeks now, Shanti Tamang has been turning bare displacement centres into something children can recognise: a place with drawing paper, playtime, and an adult trained to notice when a child needs more than a meal and a blanket. Her organisation, the Shanti Foundation , moved fast — child-friendly spaces went up in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot settlements within days of the flood, built for kids who lost their homes, and in some cases, their parents.

The scale of what they're up against is staggering. The 26 August flash flood tore through 32 schools, destroying 268 classrooms and disrupting learning for 9,400 students.

For families already sleeping in tents or borrowed rooms, the loss of school on top of home — and, for some, on top of a parent — has been a second collapse layered on the first.

Nepal's education ministry is now moving to catch these children before the gap widens. A new central fund, dubbed the "Scholarship Bank" , announced under the Secured Future Scholarship Scheme, promises free schooling through Grade 12 for every child displaced or orphaned by the floods, with those who lost a parent or guardian first in line.

The private sector has already answered the call: a consortium of private-school operators pledged Rs1 billion — roughly $6.62 million — enough to cover 1,000 students, through a mix of full residential scholarships and partial aid scaled to what each family can bear.

But money and enrollment forms only solve half the problem. Aid organisations on the ground say the emotional toll is just as urgent children separated from caregivers, or living in unstructured temporary settlements, face real risks of disease and exploitation that a supervised, structured space helps hold at bay.

Tamang's foundation is one of several stepping into that gap while the slower machinery of formal reunification and school enrollment grinds into motion.

The scholarship scheme's fine print — who qualifies, how fast aid reaches them — is still being worked out. And that's the crux of it: the next few weeks will decide how many of those 9,400 students walk back into a classroom before the school year simply moves on without them.

What it will take: funding for the Scholarship Bank that outlasts this first wave of private pledges, and continued support for the quieter, daily work like Tamang's that keeps children steady while everything else around them is still being rebuilt.

Charity check-in

At Smiley Movement, we like to elevate the work of charities across the world. Here are three charities whose causes align with the themes in this article.

Shanti Foundation. This Nepal-based nonprofit sets up child-friendly spaces within displacement settlements, giving children who've lost homes and parents a safe, structured place to be cared for by trained staff. Find out more .

Save the Children. This international children's charity has run programmes in Nepal since 1976 and mobilised rapidly after the August 2026 floods, working across shelter, family tracing and reunification, psychosocial support, and access to education. Find out more here.

UNICEF. This UN agency has scaled up its emergency response across the flood-hit districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, tracing and reunifying unaccompanied children, dispatching education supplies, and establishing temporary learning spaces for the tens of thousands of school-age children whose education was disrupted. title: Marie Colvin Center Enables Global Connections Amid Deadly Floods in Nepal - SBU News
description: Marie Colvin Center Enables Global Connections Amid Deadly Floods in Nepal  SBU News
publisher.title: SBU News
full_article:
Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel

When disaster struck Nepal, Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel ‘24 connected with a former visiting scholar at the Marie Colvin Center for International Reporting to obtain eyewitness testimony of the flooding for O Globo, one of Brazil’s leading newspapers.

On August 26, a glacial collapse near the Nepal-China border triggered flash floods, mudslides and debris flow. The impact of the collapse was equivalent to an M5.2 earthquake. More than 1,300 people were killed in Nepal and Tibet, with approximately 5,000 people missing.

Cruvinel traveled to Nepal as a foreign reporter in the Colvin Center’s 2024 Journalism Without Walls program . The visit was coordinated by Shraddha Verma, a Colvin international scholar in Fall 2023 .

Cruvinel is based in Rio de Janeiro for a training program at O Globo . Working as a journalist, he reached out to Verma, who worked until recently as an expert in child trafficking issues and an advocate for young women’s rights in Nepal.

Rafael Fonseca Cruvinel’s story in O Globo .

“Shraddha was able to help me, and a few hours later I was talking to two people impacted by the floods. My report ended up going in the print paper, as well as being posted online,” said Cruvinel.

While a journalism student at Stony Brook, Cruvinel won a Hearst Journalism Award in feature writing and was managing editor of The Stony Brook Press . After graduating from the School of Communication and Journalism, Cruvinel completed a master’s degree in publishing at New York University before returning to his native Brazil.

“I am proud of the global connections the Colvin Center has been able to foster,” said Sarah Baxter, director of the Colvin Center. “Rafael is an outstanding trilingual journalist who is making the most of the skills and contacts he acquired through Stony Brook.”

The Center’s Journalism Without Walls program has granted foreign reporting opportunities for students in Berlin , Sweden , Moldova , Kenya and Korea . Next summer’s destination will be Argentina.

Colvin international scholars have been hosted from Cambodia, Slovakia , Ukraine , Moldova , Indonesia and the West Bank through the IREX Community Solutions program.

— Melanie Formosa

The death toll in Nepal flash floods climbed to 1,399 on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) as more bodies were recovered from the eight affected districts, authorities said.

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

Nepal, Indian teams near final stage of Chilime tunnel rescue operation

According to the latest data released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 364 bodies were recovered from Chitwan district, 232 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West, and 202 from Nuwakot.

Similarly, 189 bodies were recovered from Rasuwa, 78 from Gorkha, 72 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahun.

Two others died while undergoing treatment in Kathmandu.

India approves expedited export of electricity to flood-hit Nepal

The joint command of security personnel is continuing its search and rescue operations, with the number of missing people estimated to be 5,170.

A total of 13,742 people have been rescued so far, officials said.

title: Nepal and China are still struggling to recover after the massive high-altitude glacier collapse that killed thousands - Earth.com
description: Nepal and China are still struggling to recover after the massive high-altitude glacier collapse that killed thousands  Earth.com
publisher.title: Earth.com
full_article:
A wall of ice, mud and rock tore through the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, 2026. The official death toll has now reached roughly 1,400 people, with over 5,000 more still listed as missing.

Scientists say the disaster raises hard questions about a warming world. This may be evidence of a new category of mountain risk, one that reaches far beyond the Himalayas.

What happened at Rasuwagadhi

The disaster struck when a large section of glacier broke away high above the Lhende river in Tibet’s Xizang region.

The falling ice and rock dammed the river below. When the blockage gave way shortly afterward, the surge tore through settlements in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. The flood’s power destroyed homes, hydropower plants, and border infrastructure.

The resulting avalanche struck the river roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, a critical trade route linking Nepal and China.

The debris flow and flooding travelled nearly 60 miles (100 kilometers) downstream along the Lende Khola and Trishuli Khola rivers. This is according to the U.S. Geological Survey, which is mapping the disaster’s extent using before-and-after satellite imagery of Nepal.

The initial glacier sat on a cliff about 16,000 feet (4,900 meters) high, and the resulting debris avalanche slid roughly 6,000 feet (1,800 meters) down the slope.

The collapse released so much energy it registered as the equivalent of a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. A subsequent second event roughly three hours later was equivalent to magnitude 4.2.

Rising toll in Nepal-Tibet disaster

The human cost has climbed steadily in the days since. In Nepal, authorities have confirmed the disaster has claimed at least 1,386 lives with 5,130 people still missing. Chinese authorities in the Tibet Autonomous Region have reported 43 dead and 519 missing.

More than 7,500 people have been rescued so far, including over 200 foreign nationals.

Many of those unaccounted for are pilgrims and hydropower workers. Rasuwagadhi serves as the main overland gateway to Tibet for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage, and late August falls during its peak season.

At least 19 bridges and roughly 25 miles (40 kilometers) of road have been destroyed, cutting off already remote mountain communities and hampering rescue efforts.

The danger may not have passed yet

A few days ago, Nepal issued an alert about a large body of water that had formed in China’s Tibet region following the initial collapse.

Scientists say a second failure at the same site is a real possibility. Removing one section of a glacier or slope often leaves the surrounding terrain unstable.

“Once you take a piece of mountain away, then there’s probably another piece right beside it that’s been destabilized by the removal. And so you could have a similar thing collapse,” said Simon Cox, a principal scientist at New Zealand’s GNS Science research institute.

“You may well have more material to fall down right from up at the source area, and the same thing could happen immediately again.”

Why the Himalayas

Scientists caution that not every mountain range faces the same odds of a disaster this large. Etienne Berthier, a glaciologist at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), said the scale seen in Nepal has specific regional drivers.

“They reach such proportions in the Himalayas because the terrain and the region’s high tectonic activity amplify the likelihood of such events occurring on that scale,” Berthier explained.

Other regions, such as Alaska, have similarly volatile glaciers. However, such collapses there tend to happen in completely uninhabited areas, sparing them the human toll seen in Nepal.

Still, the broader trend concerns researchers well beyond South Asia.

Tristram Hales, a professor of environmental hazards at Cardiff University, pointed to a clear pattern building over the past decade.

“We have seen a dramatic increase in the number of extremely hazardous flows such as this globally in the past decade or so,” Hales said, citing recent events in both the Himalayas and Switzerland.

Warning signs in the Alps

Researchers say rockfalls and landslides tied to thawing permafrost, itself accelerated by climate change, are becoming more common than the kind of full-scale glacial collapse seen in Nepal.

The danger to people grows sharply wherever towns, roads, or tourist sites sit nearby.

Ludovic Ravanel, a geomorphologist at the CNRS, said this year’s extreme summer heat already produced a record number of rockfalls across the Alps. Some of these were fatal, and the vast majority were attributable to the climate crisis.

In Switzerland, the municipality of Randa has been on edge over a possible glacier collapse in the days ahead. The 400 residents have been establishing safety perimeters after a string of rockfalls in the area.

Some events harder to predict in advance

Berthier said the Nepal disaster was probably very difficult to predict in advance. Researchers will need to comb through the weeks and months beforehand to determine whether any signs of instability were visible.

Glacial lake outburst floods, in contrast, tend to give more warning. These floods happen when glacier-fed lakes drain suddenly and catastrophically. Unlike a sudden slope collapse, the lakes themselves can be tracked over time.

Bernard Francou is a retired glaciologist and former research director at the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD). He said the Alps benefit from exactly that kind of oversight.

“We are well-equipped, we monitor these lakes and check for risks of overflowing or sudden drainage,” he said.

Resisting the rush to blame climate change

Despite the obvious parallels being drawn, several scientists urged caution about pinning the Nepal disaster on climate change without more evidence.

The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental institute focused on the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, struck a careful tone.

“While climate change is altering glaciers, snow conditions, permafrost, and mountain slopes across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, it is too early to determine what role climate change played in this specific event,” the organization said.

Confirming that link would require what scientists call an attribution study. This is a formal analysis comparing how likely an event like this would be in today’s fossil-fuel-warmed climate versus the climate before industrialization.

Until that work is done, researchers say the broader trend – more frequent and more hazardous mountain collapses worldwide – is clear even if any single event resists easy explanation.

Information from various news sources and the USGS.

title: How 2015 Earthquake Lessons Guide Response to Nepal’s Recent “Himalayan Tsunami” - Direct Relief

full_article:
How 2015 Earthquake Lessons Guide Response to Nepal's Recent "Himalayan Tsunami"

By Noah Smith

After the August 26th floods in Nepal, reports reaching Gordon Willcock in Kathmandu described families who had lost more than their homes. Willcock, Direct Relief's Asia Pacific regional director, said that many farmers had lost what they knew as their land, after river valleys were buried in mud and silt.

Willcock, who was also on the ground after the devastating 2015 earthquakes in Nepal, which killed more than 8,000 people, described some key differences between the two disasters. With the August floods, given the scale of transformation, some communities might have to relocate altogether.

"In an earthquake, buildings in a localized area are destroyed, but then you can rebuild. In this disaster, it's not like you can excavate and rebuild your house. It's done," Willcock said of the recent floods.

Both the remoteness of the impacted areas and geomorphic change introduced new challenges compared to the capital city-based earthquakes. Revealingly, locals felt the term "flood" failed to cover the totality of what occurred.

Residents called it a "Himalayan tsunami," Willcock said of the flooding and debris flow that killed more than 1,400 people. More than 5,300 remain missing.

In 2015, following an earthquake registering at least 7.8-magnitude in strength, Willcock had flown from his home in Melbourne alongside journalists and search-and-rescue teams, arriving at a chaotic Kathmandu airport.

Since Direct Relief’s network in-country at the time was sparse, much of his early work in the capital involved visiting hospitals, meeting as many relevant contacts as possible, and determining what they needed.

Many of those meetings resulted in partnerships that have spanned more than a decade. Dhulikhel Hospital was one of several groups involved in the 2015 earthquake response that deployed in the hours after the August 2026 floods with pre-positioned aid from Direct Relief.

Comparing Disaster Impacts: 2015 Earthquake vs. Recent Nepal Floods

As part of the ongoing flood response, Willcock wasn't able to go to the most devastated areas due to infrastructure damage, but benefited from the relationships he had helped originate years prior. From Kathmandu, he could gather information from organizations responding in the affected valleys and help coordinate support.

Comparing the two natural disasters, Willcock said that medical needs differed.

He recalled sustained demand for trauma care after the 2015 earthquake, including treatment for crush injuries. After the August 2026 floods’ initial emergency, displacement and interrupted access to chronic disease medications quickly became central concerns, he said.

Flood-destroyed roads in rural areas compounded nearly every need, including access to food, shelter, medicine and electricity. Damaged roads also blocked patients' access to functioning medical facilities; Dhulikhel Hospital sent doctors and surgeons by helicopter to support other hospitals and displaced people.

In a Sept. 11 update, Direct Relief reported that a Mountain Heart Nepal mission to Kalika Rural Municipality in Rasuwa district took nearly 12 hours, about twice the usual journey. The team delivered medical supplies and provided treatment and counseling.

Supplies positioned before the disaster helped local teams begin responding immediately. Dhulikhel Hospital deployed with Direct Relief emergency medical backpacks already on hand. Another 14 tons of medical aid arrived in Kathmandu on Sept. 6, including antibiotics, IV fluids and medications for chronic conditions.

Those efforts also address health risks beyond initial injuries: unsafe water, disrupted maternal care and the difficulty of maintaining treatment while displaced.

Local Partnerships Drive Rapid Emergency Medical Response

For Willcock, strong, lasting partnerships provide what he called "the best disaster preparedness we have."

Relationships established during the earthquake response, and maintained through subsequent support, allowed Direct Relief to identify needs more quickly and support organizations already reaching affected communities.

He described this response as more Nepal-led, with local charities, health workers and government agencies mobilizing rapidly. International organizations, he said, should strengthen that work and coordinate with existing authorities.

The work ahead, Willcock cautioned, would stretch far beyond the emergency. Recent mudflows and wildfires, even in wealthy California communities such as Montecito and Malibu, have taken years, he noted.

As was the case after 2015, Willcock said Direct Relief will continue to respond to requested needs from local partners, who are now helping communities through another disaster.

"One main learning as an organization is the importance of having strong long-term partnerships, which become the best disaster preparedness we have. They're the foundation from which we respond," he said.

title: Building a Palliative Care Network in Nepal: A New Model from Koshi Province - Oncodaily
description: Building a Palliative Care Network in Nepal: A New Model from Koshi Province  Oncodaily
publisher.title: Oncodaily
full_article:
In resource-constrained healthcare systems, the intersection of acute oncology care, chronic symptom burden, and advanced disease management presents a formidable challenge. Tertiary center beds and intensive care units are routinely overwhelmed by complex chronic and terminal patients whose care can be effectively optimized outside tertiary settings, yet who lack access to structured palliative support in their communities.

To bridge this critical gap, a transformative pilot workshop was organized by the Nepal Hospice Care Center (NHCC) in collaboration with B.P. Koirala Institute of Health Sciences (BPKIHS),supported by Two Worlds Cancer Collaboration (TWCC), Canada, bringing together frontline doctors and nurses from all 14 districts of Koshi Province.

The Hub-and-Spoke Ecosystem, with BPKIHS serving as the central hub, is developing a decentralized, four-pillar framework designed to expand palliative care expertise across the province:

Home-Based Hospice and Palliative Care: Dedicated regional clinical teams providing holistic symptom management and compassionate support directly in community settings. Intensive Workforce Capacity Building: Evidence-based training in symptom control, pain management, opioid protocols, and compassionate communication. Telemedicine & Referral Networks: A permanent digital cord connecting district health workers with tertiary specialists for real-time case consultations. Mobile Outreach & Field Mentorship: Direct on-site mentorship across the 14 districts to supervise community nurses and ensure quality delivery.

Optimizing Bed Triage and Human Dignity Beyond compassionate patient support, the model serves as an indispensable tool for healthcare resource optimization. By empowering trained physicians and community nurses to manage complex symptom trajectories and advanced illness locally, the program aims to reduce potentially avoidable hospital and ICU admissions and ease pressure on inpatient services.

A nation-wide sustainable framework developed by Dr. Soniya Dulal under the expert mentorship of Prof. Dr. Bishnu Dutta Paudel and supported by global expertise from the Two Worlds Cancer Collaboration (TWCC), the initiative is powered by strong multi-sectoral synergy between the Koshi Provincial Government and the Dharan Sub-Metropolitan City.

This project demonstrates that decentralized palliative care is not merely an ethical imperative—it is an operational necessity. As Koshi Province establishes this regional network, it lays the cornerstone for a scalable, sustainable national model across Nepal.

title: Nepal-China border flood death toll hits 1,442 - Yeni Safak English

publisher.title: Yeni Safak English
full_article:
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on Tuesday that the death toll from last month's catastrophic flash floods and mudslides at the Nepal-China border has climbed to 1,442, with rescuers recovering 14 additional bodies from the flood-hit areas. The agency stated that 1,399 bodies have been recovered from Nepalese territories alone, while 5,179 individuals are still missing there.

Authorities have rescued 13,742 people and deployed 21,022 security personnel for ongoing search, rescue and relief operations. Among the missing in Nepal are 587 foreign tourists, officials said, adding that the figure remains subject to verification and may include unidentified bodies already recovered or individuals since rescued.

Cross-border devastation

On the Chinese side, the death toll stands at 43, with 519 people still missing in Tibet — which Beijing designates as the Xizang autonomous region — including 261 foreign nationals. The catastrophe struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), triggering an ice-rock avalanche that transformed into a massive debris flow.

Floodwaters and mudslides subsequently swept through valleys along the border, devastating Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts as well as the Kathmandu Valley. The torrent also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang under tons of rock and ice, cutting off a key trade and transit point between the two nations.

title: UNC Charlotte Expert Explains Recovery Challenges After Nepal’s Catastrophic Flooding | Newswise - Newswise
description: UNC Charlotte Expert Explains Recovery Challenges After Nepal’s Catastrophic Flooding | Newswise  Newswise
publisher.title: Newswise
full_article:
Newswise — Catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border in August claimed hundreds of lives, decimated entire communities and damaged critical infrastructure. While the immediate damage is clear, it will take time before the devastation is completely understood. The individuals and communities affected have a long road of recovery ahead.

Stephanie Pilkington, UNC Charlotte assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering, and expert on natural hazards, recovery modeling and community resilience, explains the long-term challenges communities face after major flooding events, why mountainous regions are especially vulnerable and how AI and data science may help other countries around the world better prepare for natural disasters.

Beyond the immediate loss of life, what are the biggest long-term challenges communities face after catastrophic flooding?

Rebuilding. This flooding event was also a landslide and mudslide event and brought debris and soil into places it was not originally. Not only will communities have to rebuild structures, but before they can do that, they will have to move a significant amount of earth and debris.

What makes flash floods in mountainous regions especially dangerous?

One cubic foot box of water weighs a little over 60 pounds. Rivers carry more water than just one cubic foot and in mountainous regions, steep slopes cause that water to move very quickly, which, in turn, results in a very high force (or pressure) that can be exerted on the riverbanks and any nearby infrastructure. This moving water can be so powerful that it could alter a river’s course once the water recedes.



On the human development aspect of hazards, we have historically built communities in valleys and along rivers for the ease of access to water and for establishing trade routes. This is a very common practice worldwide and as we continue to develop and learn about our environment and climate, these communities will require additional work to mitigate impacts.

Why are roads, bridges and utility systems often among the first critical services to fail during disasters?

In short, their exposure lends them to being in the most vulnerable position. Bridges are how we cross waterways. Roads, and underground utilities, are dependent on the subsurface (soil) remaining intact, which, in flooding conditions, can become questionable. Aboveground utilities are very exposed to the elements and these often long thin members (e.g., poles, cables) are naturally less stable than a short, wide, box of a building when exposed to fluid forces (e.g., water, wind).

What are the economic consequences of large-scale flooding for a region?

I do not know that we can comprehend the scale of the economic impact just yet. Given that this event also occurred along the border of two countries, this will have local and international economic impacts that will take time to appear.

How can advances in data science, artificial intelligence and hazard modeling improve disaster preparedness?

In all honesty, in this specific event, I am at a loss for words. However, in considering overall, worldwide improvements to disaster preparedness, advancements in data science allow us to leverage information we have been gathering for years regarding the formation of hazards and their impacts. That is to say that advanced computing power, data storage, and yes, artificial intelligence, if used properly, could aid experts in meteorology, hazard mitigation, infrastructure, and emergency management, in discovering new patterns and solutions to help us move forward in our understanding and preparedness practices. Sometimes these data sets are so large that the use of AI can help experts “see the forest through the trees.” It is another tool now available to us and many agencies are already using it.

title: 19 Newsmakers episode 16: NEOMED leaders discuss Nepal relief effort, new programs - Cleveland 19 News
description: 19 Newsmakers episode 16: NEOMED leaders discuss Nepal relief effort, new programs  Cleveland 19 News
publisher.title: Cleveland 19 News
full_article:
CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO) - Every Monday, 19 News anchor Brian Duffy interviews the people shaping the present and future of Northeast Ohio.

This week’s edition of “19 Newsmakers” features the Northeast Ohio Medical University, or NEOMED, and its global programs, which are in the news amid an ongoing crisis in Nepal following flooding that killed more than a thousand people.

NEOMED has a long-standing relationship with Nepal, having built educational, research and global operations in the country for decades.

Dr. Bernhard Fassl, director of NEOMED’s Center for Global Health Innovation, is organizing a team of doctors and other health professionals and students who will travel to Nepal to assist with recovery and the rebuilding of water and health care infrastructure. Fassl and some team members plan to leave in the near future. NEOMED students will follow once conditions stabilize and are safer for them to be in the country.

University’s global mission

Dr. John Langell, president of NEOMED, joined “19 Newsmakers” and explained the university’s global mission, which he said creates opportunities for students to serve and to learn how health care can be delivered, including understanding deficiencies that may be in place. He said that knowledge is later used to help improve health care in a cost-effective way in the United States.

Langell said the group’s mission in Nepal will be different this time.

“Our focus and our mission there will be really attuned to medical infrastructure and care, both the acute assistance, with getting those who need care now taken care of, as well as re-establishing a footprint to deliver health care,” Langell said. “And the other that we have been assigned is clean water.”

New programs at NEOMED

Also in this edition of “19 Newsmakers,” Langell discusses new programs in nursing, dentistry and mental health that are showing signs of success and promise, which may be part of the reason enrollment is surging at NEOMED.

description: Nepal’s Judicial Council appoints judges to high courts while leaving Supreme Court vacancies unfilled  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the Judicial Council has begun filling vacancies in the high courts while leaving four positions unfilled at the Supreme Court, where about 29,000 cases are pending. This was reported by The Kathmandu Post.

At a meeting chaired by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma, the council appointed Bhadrakali Pokharel, Himlal Belbase and Gajendra Bahadur Singh as high court judges in Surkhet, Janakpur and Biratnagar, respectively. Belbase is due to retire on age grounds in four days, while Pokharel was appointed a judge on the eve of his retirement from the post of Supreme Court registrar.

Supreme Court administrative official Bharat Kumar Dahal was also appointed a district court judge and assigned to the Kailali District Court. The council transferred several other judges to high and district courts.

Supreme Court workload

On Tuesday, 489 cases were listed for hearing at the Supreme Court. Decisions were made in 230 of them, while 259 were postponed for various reasons, including the impossibility or impracticality of hearing them. Constitutionally, the court must consist of 21 judges including the chief justice, but only 17 are currently serving. Justice Binod Sharma is due to retire on age grounds next month, which will further reduce the court’s composition.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Kedar Koirala, general secretary of the Nepal Bar Association, criticized the sequence of appointments. According to him, the council resolved an administrative matter rather than the judiciary’s most urgent problem, since the shortage of Supreme Court judges directly affects parties to court proceedings.

Further personnel decisions

Manoj Kumar Sharma said that the appointment process had already begun and vacancies at all levels of the judiciary would soon be filled. At the same time, a member of the Judicial Council told the publication that appointments of Supreme Court judges and chief judges of high courts were unlikely to take place before October 1.

Full appointments to the Supreme Court have not been made for several years. In June 2025, the Judicial Council recommended Meghraj Pokharel for the post of Supreme Court justice, but one vacancy remained unfilled at that time. Subsequently, Justices Kumar Chudal and Prakash Man Singh Raut retired in October 2025 and April 2026, respectively. The Judicial Council Act of 2016 provides for recommending candidates at least one month before a judge’s planned age-based retirement.

After the meeting, the Judicial Service Commission also recommended Baburam Dahal and Thagindra Kattel for the posts of Supreme Court registrars, and Rama Prasad Bhattarai for the post of Judicial Council secretary. These appointments will take effect after government approval.

full_article:
MARY SHEPHERD SLUSSER landed in Kathmandu on 13 November 1965. She was carrying a typewriter, a pair of cats named Latsa and Bratsa, and two Persian rugs she had purchased in Tehran during a layover on her flight from Washington DC. Her husband, Harry Robert (“Bob”) Slusser, had been appointed the local deputy director of the Investment Generation Division at the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). He would help Nepal manage its timber, electrify its cities and solicit foreign investment for tourism projects.

Slusser was astounded at the beauty of her new home. She “almost screamed, yelled, and fell out of the car” as the couple drove through the centre of Kathmandu on the way to their new apartment, passing “temples and stupas and shrines and houses jumbled together and sprinkled with hill peoples, holy men, sacred cattle, scrawny dogs, scavenger pigs and heaven knows what.” In her first letter home, Slusser described Nepal as being “beyond our wildest dreams.”

Slusser bought her first stolen gods just a few weeks after she arrived. Taking a Sunday sight-seeing drive, the Slussers stopped at the Gokarneshwor Mahadev temple, dedicated to the Hindu deity Shiva, on the northeastern edge of the Kathmandu Valley. On the wide steps leading down from the temple to the Bagmati River, Slusser recorded in her diary, families were picnicking, little girls were washing brass pots and “some sort of esoteric ceremony” was in progress, “with much mutual blessings.”

As the Slussers lingered in the temple complex’s courtyard, some boys showed them a tiny bronze sculpture of Shiva and his consort, Parvati. Slusser was “sure they had just stolen” this idol, since grains of rice, offered to the gods by their worshippers, were still clinging to its surface.

Thanks to Slusser’s intensive Nepali lessons, she understood that the boys were asking for NPR 22 for the sculpture. She bargained them down to NPR 14 – then the equivalent of USD 1.82, as she noted with customary exactitude in her diary. “It is really a very sweet piece,” she added, “and I don’t think the temple will miss it at all.”
